summary: Radar for 17 Nov 2026, GLP-1 focus. Three things drive today's news. (1) The FDA's NAION eye warning is spreading to consumer outlets. Medscape, Business Standard and Best Life all covered it on 17 Nov, and the label section names Mounjaro and Zepbound too. (2) The Washington Post's 'serious complications of GLP-1s' piece (16 Nov) is a good hook for the queued 'Serious Risks: How Rare?' long video. (3) ObesityWeek is wrapping up. It brought SURMOUNT-ADOLESCENTS (JAMA, 15 Nov), EloraTZP in type 2 diabetes being presented again, the Wegovy pill's 6.2% real-world result, and 'why GLP-1s don't work for everyone' coverage (The Conversation, 16 Nov). Stopping is also back in the news: an observational study in The Lancet Regional Health Europe (80,302 adults with type 2 diabetes) linked stopping to about double the rate of heart attack, stroke or death. It is being widely reported as 'quitting doubled heart attack and stroke'. Use it only as a hook for the stopping and keeping-results videos, never as the topic, and never as advice to keep taking or stop the drug. One gap almost nobody has covered: 'skin hurts' (allodynia). Pharmacy Times wrote about it on 16 Nov, but the trial data is for semaglutide only, and tirzepatide has only case reports so far. Following the growth playbook, the top long-form picks are broad searched questions: the holiday table (as Shorts linked to Thanksgiving), the eye-warning label change, Serious Risks, Mounjaro vs Zepbound, Weight Loss in the Trials, why results vary, Months 2–6, and keeping results. Rejected: dose-escalation and 'staying on low doses' stories, the TiTRE titration protocol, switching between semaglutide and tirzepatide, retatrutide 'supplier' and seizure stories, pricing, Medicaid and CVS stories, and microdosing.

candidates.topic: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound) and the FDA's new eye warning (NAION): what changed on the label and how rare it is
candidates.angle: A label-change long video titled 'Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) Eye Warning: How Rare Is It?'. Give the FDA rate first (about 6.4 vs 3.8 per 100,000 person-years), then explain what NAION is and which symptoms mean you should seek help right away: sudden, painless vision loss in one eye, often on waking. Keep the tone calm and practical: rare, but know the signs. Cite NANOS and the AAO by name. Never say 'stop the drug'; tell viewers to contact their prescriber.
candidates.why_now: The story has moved from clinician outlets (Medscape, 17 Nov) to consumer ones (Best Life and Business Standard, 17 Nov), and the warning applies to every GLP-1, tirzepatide included. Label changes are one of the formats that beat our usual views by 10x or more. Most consumer coverage names only Ozempic and Wegovy, so a tirzepatide-first video fills a gap.

evidence.source: Medscape, 17 Nov: 'GLP-1s and NAION: What Clinicians Should Know'
evidence.signal: Clinician coverage on the day

candidates.topic: Stopping tirzepatide: what happens to weight and heart risk? SURMOUNT-4, plus the new 'stopping linked to double the heart attack and stroke rate' study (type 2 diabetes, observational)
candidates.angle: Use the news as the hook, with the scope stated plainly. It was an observational Italian cohort of 80,302 adults with type 2 diabetes: about 4 vs 2 events per 100 people a year. It shows a link, not cause and effect, and it may not apply to people taking the drug only for weight. Pair it with SURMOUNT-4 (335 vs 335; +14.0% regain on placebo, still 9.9% below baseline). Close with 'any change should be planned with your prescriber'. Best used as a pinned-comment or community refresh of the Stopping and Keeping Results videos and as a re-hook chapter. Not a new topic for a Short.
